teach.title: Something is done to the subject
teach.say: Up to now the subject has been the one doing: *māter Mārcum vocat*, mother calls Marcus. Turn it round and Marcus becomes the subject with the calling done to him: *Mārcus vocātur*. That is **the passive (the 'is done' form)**. English needs two words, *is called*; Latin changes the end of the one verb.

check.ask: Which word says that something is being done to the slave?

teach.title: One subject: -tur
teach.say: Where the active verb ends -t, the passive ends -tur: *vocat* he calls → *vocātur* he is called; *pulsat* → *pulsātur*; *salūtat* → *salūtātur*. Two letters go on the end, and the vowel in front of them stretches as they do: the short -a- of *vocat* becomes the long -ā- of *vocātur*. The same stretch happens in *vidētur* and *audītur*.

show.say: vocātur — one person, and it is being done to him

check.ask: Give the form meaning 'he is called'.

teach.title: More than one subject: -ntur
teach.say: Where the active ends -nt, the passive ends -ntur: *vocant* they call → *vocantur* they are called; *portant* → *portantur*. The -ur is the passive part in both, and the n says there is more than one.

show.say: vocantur — more than one, and it is being done to them

check.ask: Give the form meaning 'they are called'.

teach.title: Read the tail: -t or -tur
teach.say: The two sit side by side in the same sentence often enough that the tail is worth reading twice. *Vocat* — he calls somebody. *Vocātur* — somebody calls him. The subject is nominative either way: it is *servus vocātur*, never *servum*.

check.ask: Of *portant* and *portantur*, which one has the girls doing the carrying?

teach.title: Who does it, and what it is done with
teach.say: A passive verb can name the doer with *ā* (or *ab* before a vowel) and the ablative: *ā servīs portātur*, he is carried by slaves. A thing is different: it takes the bare ablative with no *ā* at all, because it is the means, not the doer — *rosīs dēlectātur*, she is delighted by roses.

check.ask: Is *rosīs* the one doing it, or the thing she is delighted by, and what tells you?

teach.title: The other conjugations
teach.say: Every verb makes the passive the same way, with its own vowel in front: *vidētur* is seen, *audītur* is heard, *audiuntur* are heard. Consonant stems keep the i and u they use in the active: *pōnit* → *pōnitur*, *sūmunt* → *sūmuntur*, *carpunt* → *carpuntur*. (*Vidētur* also does duty for 'it seems'; in *Vīlla Iūliī ex oppidō vidētur* the *ex oppidō* settles which one is meant.)

show.say: sūmitur / sūmuntur — the -ur goes on behind the active vowel

check.ask: Give 'it is taken' and 'they are taken'.

core.text: So far the subject has done the action: *servī dominum portant* = the slaves carry the master. Turn it round and the master becomes the subject and has it done to him: *dominus ā servīs portātur* = the master is carried by the slaves. That is **the passive (the 'is done' form)**, *genus passīvum*. Latin makes it with new endings: -tur for one (*portātur*), -ntur for several (*portantur*).

Active: *the dog bites the man*. Passive: *the man is bitten (by the dog)*. English adds *is / are* plus a participle (a verb used like an adjective); Latin changes the ending and needs no helping verb.
Replace -t with -tur and -nt with -ntur: *vocat → vocātur*, *vocant → vocantur*. Only a verb that can take an object can be passive.

invented.en: The boy is called by his mother.
The roses are picked by the girls.

core.text: *Vocat* — he calls (he is doing it). *Vocātur* — he is called (it is done to him). The -ur tail is the whole difference, and it flips who acts. The subject of a passive verb is nominative all the same: *puer vocātur*, not *puerum*.

more.text: From the learner's notes: 'voice' is the relation between the subject and the action — doing it (active) or receiving it (passive). The notes' variable vowels again: consonant stems keep them (*pōnitur, pōnuntur*; *dūcitur, dūcuntur*), a- and e-stems drop them (*aedificātur, aedificantur*; *vidētur, videntur*), i-stems drop the i in the singular but keep the u in the plural (*accipitur, accipiuntur*; *audītur, audiuntur*). Intransitive verbs — states (*est*, *dormit*), motion (*it*, *cadit*), self-contained action (*rīdet*) — have no object and so no passive; if you cannot add a sensible object, the verb cannot be passive.

Ørberg cap. VI: -tur / -ntur with *ā servō* for the doer. The other persons (-or, -ris, -mur, -minī) come later, and some passives read best as active English: *dēlectātur* = is pleased, likes; *vehitur* = rides. A&G §156, §163.
